title: Tiered cake assembly
subtitle: How to stack and support a two-tier or three-tier celebration cake
excerpt: A tiered cake needs an internal support structure to stop the upper tiers sinking into the lower ones. Hollow plastic or wooden dowels take the weight; a cake board between each tier spreads the load. The method is the same whether the tiers are 15 cm, 20 cm, and 25 cm or any other combination.
sourceNotes: Tiered cake construction is covered in British sugarcraft and patisserie training curricula. The dowelling and board method described here is standard professional practice, documented in celebration cake manuals from the 1980s onwards.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble the tiers the day before serving. Chill overnight to firm the buttercream, then allow to come to room temperature for 2 hours before the event.

glossaryTerms.definition: A straight rod (plastic, wooden, or metal) inserted vertically into a cake tier to carry the weight of the tier above and prevent sinking.

content.text: A tiered cake is not just a stack of cakes. Without

inside the lower tier, the upper tier slowly sinks into the soft sponge and buttercream, and the whole structure slides at the table. Each tier sits on its own board and each lower tier carries a ring of dowels that bear the load.

For each tier you need: a cake board or drum the same size as the tier (so the tier sits flush, not protruding), hollow plastic or wooden dowels, a pencil, a craft knife or strong scissors. The bottom tier sits on a drum that is at least 5 cm larger all around than the tier itself.
Place the cake board for the next tier on top of the lower tier and trace lightly around it with a skewer or toothpick. This marks the area the upper tier will cover.

Insert four to five dowels in a ring inside the traced circle, spaced evenly. Push each dowel straight down until it touches the board beneath the cake. Mark the dowel level with the top of the cake, pull it out, and cut all remaining dowels to the same height.
Reinsert all cut dowels. The tops should sit level with the top surface of the tier. Avoid leaving any proud of the surface; trim them slightly shorter if needed.
Spread a small amount of buttercream or royal icing in the centre of the dowel ring. This acts as a non-slip adhesive between the board and the lower tier's frosting.
Lower the upper tier (on its board) squarely onto the lower tier. Press very gently. The weight of the tier settles the board onto the dowels.
Repeat the dowelling and stacking process for any additional tiers.
The central dowel (for three tiers or tall cakes)

For three or more tiers, or when travelling with the cake, a single long central dowel threaded through all tiers adds stability. Push it down through the centre of the top tier and each board beneath until it reaches the drum. This is especially useful if the cake will be transported before serving.

Transport tiers separately if possible and assemble on site. If the assembled cake must travel, drive slowly, keep the vehicle cool, and place the cake on a non-slip mat on a flat surface, not a seat.
